Daniel’s distinction between “writing errors” and “reading errors” usefully shifts responsibility back onto the writer, but it smuggles in a strong assumption: that most misreadings are predictable, and therefore preventable. In practice, “reading errors” come from at least three sources—(1) genuine ambiguity (the writer didn’t constrain interpretation), (2) pragmatic mismatch (the writer and reader don’t share enough context), and (3) attentional limits (the prose is correct but too costly to parse). Lumping these together risks making the prescription feel harsher than it needs to be: some “errors” are best fixed by tightening syntax, others by explicitly stating premises, and others by re-chunking information so working memory isn’t overloaded. This is close to H. P. Grice’s cooperative principle—especially the maxims of manner and quantity—where clarity is not merely correctness but an active management of how readers infer meaning ([Grice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Grice)).

On “unique words,” Daniel is right that length isn’t the sin; abstraction and cliché-abstraction are. But the critique could be sharper if it named the underlying failure mode: nominalization and “meta-concept” language often hides who did what to whom, when, and why. George Orwell’s advice isn’t “use short words,” it’s “prefer concrete, verifiable phrasing that resists self-deception”—because vague abstractions don’t just bore; they insulate claims from being tested or contradicted ([Orwell, *Politics and the English Language*](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/the-orwell-foundation/orwell/essays-and-other-works/politics-and-the-english-language/)). If Daniel wants a practical upgrade, the rule could be: whenever a meta-word appears (“leverage,” “paradigm,” “impact,” “framework”), force it to cash out in an observable action, a specific agent, and a falsifiable claim; otherwise the prose isn’t merely unreadable—it’s unaccountable.
